# Advanced Pandas: Grouping, Merging, and Reshaping ##### The merge that created 340,000 rows from 12,000 An analyst at an edtech company in Hyderabad joined a students table (12,000 rows) to an enrolments table (18,000 rows). The result had 340,000 rows. She assumed Pandas was broken. It was not. Her students table had duplicate `student_id` values — the same student appearing three or four times because of a bad data import. The enrolments table had multiple rows per student, correctly. When both sides have duplicates on the join key, every match on the left pairs with every match on the right, and row counts multiply. The one-line diagnostic she should have run first: ```python print(students["student_id"].duplicated().sum()) # 2,847 <- there it is ``` Merges are where beginners lose the most time and trust the wrong numbers. Combined with `groupby` and reshaping, they are also the three operations that turn a raw table into an actual answer. Today covers all three, with the failure modes. ##### groupby: split, apply, combine The mental model, from Hadley Wickham's split-apply-combine framing, is exactly three steps: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Full DataFrame] --> B[SPLIT into groups
by one or more keys] B --> C1[Group: North] B --> C2[Group: South] B --> C3[Group: West] C1 --> D[APPLY a function
sum, mean, count...] C2 --> D C3 --> D D --> E[COMBINE into one result] ``` ```python import pandas as pd, numpy as np orders = pd.DataFrame({ "order_id": range(1001, 1013), "customer_id": [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 1, 5, 3, 2, 4, 5], "region": ["North","South","North","West","South","North", "North","West","West","South","North","West"], "category": ["Books","Electronics","Books","Apparel","Books", "Electronics","Apparel","Books","Electronics","Apparel", "Books","Electronics"], "amount_inr": [1200, 45000, 800, 2300, 1500, 38000, 3100, 950, 27000, 1800, 640, 52000], "units": [2, 1, 1, 3, 2, 1, 4, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1], }) # Single column, single aggregation print(orders.groupby("region")["amount_inr"].sum()) # Multiple aggregations print(orders.groupby("region")["amount_inr"].agg(["sum", "mean", "count", "max"])) # Named aggregation — the clearest form, and gives you sensible column names summary = orders.groupby("region").agg( total_revenue=("amount_inr", "sum"), avg_order=("amount_inr", "mean"), order_count=("order_id", "count"), unique_customers=("customer_id", "nunique"), total_units=("units", "sum"), ).round(2).reset_index() print(summary) # Group by several keys print(orders.groupby(["region", "category"])["amount_inr"].sum()) # Custom function print(orders.groupby("region")["amount_inr"].agg(lambda s: s.quantile(0.9))) ``` **Named aggregation** (`total_revenue=("amount_inr", "sum")`) is worth adopting as your default. The alternative produces a MultiIndex on the columns that is awkward to work with, and `reset_index()` turns the group keys back into ordinary columns. Three related methods that beginners often miss: ```python # transform: returns a value per ROW, not per group — perfect for new columns orders["region_total"] = orders.groupby("region")["amount_inr"].transform("sum") orders["pct_of_region"] = (orders["amount_inr"] / orders["region_total"] * 100).round(1) # filter: keep whole groups meeting a condition big_regions = orders.groupby("region").filter(lambda g: g["amount_inr"].sum() > 50000) # apply: full flexibility, slowest — use only when agg/transform cannot do it def top_two(g): return g.nlargest(2, "amount_inr")[["order_id", "amount_inr"]] print(orders.groupby("region", group_keys=True).apply(top_two, include_groups=False)) ``` `transform` is the one that unlocks a whole class of analysis — "what share of its region's revenue is this order?" needs a group-level number attached back to every row, and `transform` does exactly that. One argument to know: `observed=True` when grouping categorical columns. Without it, Pandas produces every combination of categories including ones with no data, which can turn a 20-row result into thousands of empty rows. ##### Merging and joining A merge combines two tables by matching values in a key column. ```python customers = pd.DataFrame({ "customer_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 6], "name": ["Ananya", "Rahul", "Meera", "Vikram", "Sneha"], "city": ["Pune", "Mumbai", "Pune", "Nashik", "Nagpur"], "joined": pd.to_datetime(["2024-03-01","2024-06-15","2025-01-10", "2025-04-22","2025-09-05"]), }) merged = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left") print(merged.head()) ``` The `how` argument is the decision that matters: | how | Keeps | Use when | |---|---|---| | `inner` | Only rows matching in **both** | You need complete records | | `left` | All left rows; `NaN` where no match | Enriching a primary table | | `right` | All right rows | Rare — flip the tables instead | | `outer` | Everything from both | Reconciliation, finding gaps | ``` orders.customer_id: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 customers.customer_id: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 inner -> 1, 2, 3, 4 (customer 5 and 6 dropped) left -> 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (customer 5 has NaN name) outer -> 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (both gaps visible) ``` **`left` is the right default for enrichment.** You have a table of orders and you want customer details attached; using `inner` would silently delete orders whose customer is missing from the customer table — and silently losing rows is far worse than seeing `NaN`. The habits that prevent the Hyderabad incident: ```python # 1. Check for duplicate keys BEFORE merging print(customers["customer_id"].duplicated().sum()) # should be 0 for a lookup table print(orders["customer_id"].duplicated().sum()) # expected here — many orders per customer # 2. Declare the relationship — Pandas will raise if it is violated merged = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one") # 3. Use the indicator to see what matched merged = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", indicator=True) print(merged["_merge"].value_counts()) # both 10 # left_only 2 <- orders with no customer record: investigate # 4. Check row count did not change unexpectedly assert len(merged) == len(orders), "merge changed row count — duplicate keys?" ``` `validate="many_to_one"` is the single most valuable argument in `merge`. It states your assumption, and Pandas raises an error if the data violates it. That is a bug caught in one second instead of eleven days. Other things you will need: ```python # Different column names on each side orders.merge(customers, left_on="customer_id", right_on="cust_id", how="left") # Merge on multiple keys sales.merge(targets, on=["region", "month"], how="left") # Overlapping column names get suffixed a.merge(b, on="id", suffixes=("_orders", "_returns")) ``` ##### Concatenating Merging joins **sideways** on a key. Concatenating stacks tables **vertically** (or side by side) with no matching logic. ```python jan = pd.read_csv("sales_jan.csv") feb = pd.read_csv("sales_feb.csv") mar = pd.read_csv("sales_mar.csv") # Stack rows — the common case year = pd.concat([jan, feb, mar], ignore_index=True) # Keep track of the source year = pd.concat([jan, feb, mar], keys=["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"], names=["month", "row"]) # Loading many files from pathlib import Path frames = [pd.read_csv(f).assign(source=f.stem) for f in Path("data").glob("sales_*.csv")] year = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True) ``` `ignore_index=True` matters: without it you get repeated index values (0,1,2,0,1,2,...) which breaks `.loc` in confusing ways. A trap: if the files have slightly different column names — `amount` in one and `amount_inr` in another — `concat` will happily create both columns, each half full of `NaN`. Check `df.columns` across files before concatenating, or use `verify_integrity` and explicit column selection. ##### Pivot tables A pivot table reshapes long data into a grid, with one variable as rows and another as columns. ```python pivot = orders.pivot_table( index="region", columns="category", values="amount_inr", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0, margins=True, # adds row and column totals margins_name="Total", ) print(pivot) # Multiple aggregations at once print(orders.pivot_table(index="region", columns="category", values="amount_inr", aggfunc=["sum", "count"], fill_value=0)) ``` `pivot_table` aggregates; the simpler `pivot` does not and will raise an error on duplicate index/column combinations. In practice you almost always want `pivot_table`. Note that a pivot table and a `groupby` on two keys contain the same information in different shapes — grouped output is long and good for further computation, pivoted output is wide and good for reading. ##### Melt: wide to long `melt` is the inverse of pivot, and it is how you convert a spreadsheet-shaped table into the "tidy" format that plotting and modelling libraries expect. ```python wide = pd.DataFrame({ "region": ["North", "South", "West"], "Q1": [125000, 98000, 143000], "Q2": [131000, 105000, 138000], "Q3": [118000, 112000, 156000], }) long = wide.melt(id_vars="region", var_name="quarter", value_name="revenue_inr") print(long) # region quarter revenue_inr # 0 North Q1 125000 # 1 South Q1 98000 # ... ``` Wickham's **tidy data** principles are worth internalising, because they explain *why* long format keeps appearing: 1. Each variable is a column. 2. Each observation is a row. 3. Each type of observational unit is a table. The wide table above violates rule 1 — "quarter" is a variable, but it is spread across three column *names* rather than living in a column. Seaborn, scikit-learn and most statistical tools assume tidy input, which is why `melt` shows up constantly. **Rule of thumb: long for computing and plotting, wide for humans reading a report.** ##### apply and map ```python # map: element-wise on a Series, often with a dictionary region_head = {"North": "Amit", "South": "Priya", "West": "Kiran"} orders["manager"] = orders["region"].map(region_head) orders["category_short"] = orders["category"].map(lambda s: s[:4].upper()) # apply on a Series orders["amount_k"] = orders["amount_inr"].apply(lambda x: f"₹{x/1000:.1f}k") # apply on a DataFrame, row-wise — powerful and SLOW orders["flag"] = orders.apply( lambda r: "review" if r["amount_inr"] > 40000 and r["units"] == 1 else "ok", axis=1, ) ``` The performance warning matters. `apply(axis=1)` is a Python loop wearing a Pandas costume — on 100,000 rows it can be 50–500× slower than the vectorized equivalent: ```python # Slow orders["flag"] = orders.apply(lambda r: "review" if r["amount_inr"] > 40000 else "ok", axis=1) # Fast — same result import numpy as np orders["flag"] = np.where(orders["amount_inr"] > 40000, "review", "ok") # Multiple conditions, still vectorized orders["tier"] = np.select( [orders["amount_inr"] > 40000, orders["amount_inr"] > 2000], ["premium", "standard"], default="small", ) ``` Use `np.where` for two outcomes, `np.select` for several, and reach for `apply(axis=1)` only when the logic genuinely cannot be vectorized. ##### Common mistakes - Merging without checking for duplicate keys, and silently multiplying rows. - Using `inner` when you meant `left`, and silently losing rows. - Not using `validate=` or `indicator=`, so a bad join looks fine. - Forgetting `reset_index()` after `groupby`, then being confused by the index. - `groupby` on categoricals without `observed=True`, exploding the output. - `concat` without `ignore_index=True`, producing duplicate index values. - Concatenating files with mismatched column names, creating half-empty columns. - `apply(axis=1)` on large data instead of `np.where` or `np.select`. - Using `pivot` where `pivot_table` was needed, and hitting a duplicate-entry error. - Never checking `len(df)` before and after a merge. ##### Hands-on Take two related datasets — orders and customers, or students and enrolments. Before merging, check for duplicate keys on both sides and print the counts. Merge with `how="left"`, `validate=` and `indicator=True`, then inspect the `_merge` column to see exactly which rows matched. Assert that the row count is unchanged. Then run a `groupby` with named aggregation producing at least four metrics, use `transform` to add a share-of-group column, and build a pivot table with margins. For the mini-project, combine two related public datasets and answer five specific business questions with grouped summaries and a pivot table. Write the questions first. Along the way, document every join decision — which `how` and why, what you found in the `_merge` breakdown, and how many rows were unmatched. That documentation is what makes the analysis trustworthy, and it is the part most beginner notebooks omit entirely. Finish by melting one of your wide summary tables into long format and explaining which shape you would use for a chart versus a report. For the assignment, explain inner versus left join with a small worked example where the row counts visibly differ, then show a `groupby` computing a metric per category. Add one sentence on when using `inner` would have silently hidden a data-quality problem. ##### Key takeaways - `groupby` is split-apply-combine; use named aggregation, and `transform` when you need the group value back on every row. - Always check for duplicate keys before merging — duplicates on both sides multiply rows. - `validate=` and `indicator=True` turn silent merge bugs into immediate errors and visible diagnostics. - `left` is the safe default for enrichment; `inner` silently drops rows. - Long (tidy) format for computing and plotting, wide for human reading — `melt` and `pivot_table` convert between them.
